title: Kruse v. Karlen — Appeal Dismissed and $10,000 Frivolous-Appeal Damages for AI-Fabricated Citations Filed by a Self-Represented Appellant
author: Judge Kurt S. Odenwald

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: Kruse supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI assistance does not transfer responsibility for accuracy: fabricated authorities and misrepresented holdings remain false statements to the court regardless of AI provenance. It also reinforces candour duties and applies procedural certification responsibility to self-represented litigants, though it does not address empirical error rates or the broader regulatory debate.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The court squarely supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI involvement and self-representation do not displace human responsibility for accurate filings. It relies on existing candor and briefing rules and grounds dismissal in fictitious authorities, substantial procedural violations and failure to correct—not AI use itself.

st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: Kruse supports continuing human accountability for litigation filings regardless of AI assistance or self-representation. It applies equal briefing standards to pro se litigants and grounds dismissal in significant procedural violations, consistent with the cluster’s view that consequences turn on conduct and governing authority rather than AI use alone.
qs: “[J]udicial impartiality and fairness mandate that we hold pro se appellants to the same standards as parties represented by lawyers.” Puetz, 675 S.W.3d at 656 (internal citation omitted).
The significant violations of Rule 84.04 mandate dismissal of the appeal.

st.an: The case supports the cluster’s emphasis on verification and professional accountability: AI involvement did not excuse fictitious authorities, and reliance on them was treated as an abuse of the judicial process. It is a concrete sanctions incident showing failed verification, not evidence of general model error rates or broader productivity and labour effects.

kp.k: Fabricated citations accompanied fatal briefing deficiencies
kp.d: On February 13, 2024, the Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District, dismissed Karlen's self-represented appeal because numerous substantial briefing violations prevented meaningful review, including fictitious AI-generated authorities. The disposition was not based solely on AI use: the court also identified a missing appendix, an unsigned brief, inadequate factual statements, missing Points Relied On and inaccurate tables.
qs: Due to numerous fatal briefing deficiencies under the Rules of Appellate Procedure that prevent us from engaging in meaningful review, including the submission of fictitious cases generated by artificial intelligence (“A.I.”), we dismiss the appeal.
The significant violations of Rule 84.04 mandate dismissal of the appeal.

kp.k: Citation defects included fabrication and misrepresented genuine authorities
kp.d: The court found only two of the brief's twenty-four case citations genuine; those two lacked pincites and did not support the asserted propositions. It also identified a nonexistent quotation, potentially real case names attached to incorrect authorities, and misstatements of statutes and rules. These are findings about this filing, not a measured error rate for an identified AI model.
qs: Only two out of the twenty-four case citations in Appellant's Brief are genuine.
The two genuine citations are presented in a section entitled Summary of Argument without pincites and do not stand for what Appellant purports.
Neither the case nor the specific quote it purports to contain exist in reality.
Throughout the Appellate Brief, Appellant's cited statutory and rule authorities do not state what Appellant claims.

kp.k: Cheap outsourced drafting did not excuse false submissions
kp.d: Karlen reported hiring an online consultant claiming California attorney licensure for less than one percent of the cost of retaining an attorney. He said he did not know the consultant would use AI hallucinations and denied intending to mislead the court. The court acknowledged his apology but held him responsible for the brief submitted and certified in his name; the consultant's credentials and pricing were the appellant's account, not independently established findings.
qs: In his Reply Brief, Appellant apologized for submitting fictitious cases and explained that he hired an online “consultant” purporting to be an attorney licensed in California to prepare the Appellate Brief.
Appellant indicated that the fee paid amounted to less than one percent of the cost of retaining an attorney.

Appellant stated he did not know that the individual would use “artificial intelligence hallucinations” and denied any intention to mislead the Court or waste Respondent's time researching fictitious precedent.
Appellant submitted the Appellate Brief in his name and certified its compliance with Rules 55.03 and 84.06(c) as a self-represented person.

kp.k: Existing candor duties apply to AI-generated authorities
kp.d: The court treated bogus citations as a violation of candor and an abuse of the judicial system under existing filing obligations. It invoked Missouri Rule 55.03's reasonable-inquiry certification, cited ABA Model Rule 3.3 on candor, and quoted Mata v. Avianca for the proposition that fake opinions cannot constitute existing law or support nonfrivolous legal development. AI provenance did not excuse false legal authority.
qs: Filing an appellate brief with bogus citations in this Court for any reason cannot be countenanced and represents a flagrant violation of the duties of candor Appellant owes to this Court.
A fake opinion is not “existing law” and citation to a fake opinion does not provide a non-frivolous ground for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law, or for establishing new law.
Appellant's submission of fictitious cases constitutes an abuse of the judicial system.

kp.k: False authorities impose costs on opponents and courts
kp.d: The court found that deciphering the filing and identifying fictitious authorities forced the respondent to expend additional resources. It awarded $10,000 in Rule 84.19 frivolous-appeal damages toward appellate attorneys' fees, considering both those burdens and repeated procedural failures. The court also stated that the underlying claims lacked merit even if the brief had complied with the rules, so the award should not be characterized as a standalone penalty for using AI.
qs: Appellant's actions in pursuing this appeal have required Respondent to expend more resources than necessary to decipher the record and arguments as well as to identify the fictitious cases Appellant wrongly presented to this Court.
Appellant lacked any basis for asserting error on the part of the trial court in entering summary judgment.
Appellant is hereby ordered to pay Respondent damages towards appellate attorneys’ fees in the amount of $10,000.

kp.k: Self-representation does not lower standards for legal authority
kp.d: The court acknowledged affordability barriers and the challenges of self-representation, but insisted that fairness and impartiality require the same procedural standards for represented and self-represented litigants. It distinguished reasonable accommodations from acting as a litigant's advocate and noted that successful pro se appeals had used freely accessible caselaw.
qs: And we further appreciate the challenges placed on pro se litigants who are unable to afford legal counsel.
This Court routinely makes reasonable accommodations for pro se litigants when doing so does not cause the Court to become an advocate for the pro se litigant.
Pro se appellants have successfully argued and won appeals in this Court using freely accessible caselaw.
Here, Appellant chose to retain dubious assistance and submitted fictitious and incorrect legal authorities.

kp.k: Court warns practitioners amid emerging AI filing rules
kp.d: The court described this case as its first opportunity to address fictitious cases associated with generative AI. It reported that courts nationally were considering or adopting local restrictions or disclosure requirements, and warned both lawyers and self-represented parties against fraudulent submissions. The opinion does not announce a new blanket AI prohibition or disclosure rule for this court.
qs: We regret that Appellant has given us our first opportunity to consider the impact of fictitious cases being submitted to our Court, an issue which has gained national attention in the rising availability of generative A.I.

To protect the integrity of the justice system, courts around the country have been considering and/or enacting local rules specifically geared towards prohibiting or disclosing the use of generative A.I. in court filings.
We urge all parties practicing before this Court, barred and self-represented alike, to be cognizant that we are aware of the issue and will not permit fraud on this Court in violation of our rules.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Odenwald's opinion identifies AI-fabricated legal authorities as a concrete threat to reliable court filings, imposing additional work on courts and opposing parties and exposing filers to existing procedural consequences.
pts.d: The court attributes fictitious citations in Karlen's appeal to generative AI and treats their submission as an abuse of the judicial system, notwithstanding his explanation that an online consultant prepared the brief and that he did not know AI would be used. It finds that identifying fictitious authorities increased the respondent's work. The appeal was dismissed and $10,000 in frivolous-appeal damages awarded, but those outcomes rested on numerous procedural deficiencies and the appeal's underlying lack of merit, not AI use alone. The opinion also reports that courts nationally were considering or adopting local rules prohibiting or requiring disclosure of generative AI use in filings. These are case-specific findings and a contemporary regulatory observation, not predictions of market-wide automation or lawyer displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of the court's examination of one appeal, the appellant's account of outsourced drafting, and procedural and legal authorities; it is not a model-performance study.
pts.d: Odenwald reports that only two of 24 case citations were genuine and that even those did not support the asserted propositions. The opinion supplies examples of nonexistent cases and quotations, mischaracterized cases, and erroneous statutory and rule references. Karlen's reply brief is the basis for the account of an online consultant's involvement, alleged AI use, lack of intent to mislead, and a fee below one percent of retaining an attorney; that fee comparison is the appellant's report, not independently established evidence of AI cost savings. The court also relies on Missouri procedural rules and frivolous-appeal precedents, cites Mata v. Avianca as an analogous incident, and invokes commentary and Model Rule 3.3 on candor. The citation count describes this filing, not a general hallucination rate. The supplied text references an itemized chart but does not reproduce it.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The opinion addresses harms already observed by February 13, 2024, and warns that existing filing obligations apply to future submissions by lawyers and self-represented parties alike.
pts.d: The court characterizes this as its first occasion to address fictitious cases submitted to it amid growing generative AI availability. Its warning concerns fabricated or inaccurate authorities in court filings, rather than declaring all AI-assisted drafting impermissible. The court applies Missouri procedural rules identified as the 2023 rules, including certification based on reasonable inquiry, without excusing a filer because a consultant produced the work. Frivolous-appeal damages remain discretionary and case-specific. The opinion sets no forecast horizon for broader AI adoption or legal-market change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are self-represented litigants, lawyers filing briefs, opposing parties and their counsel, and courts required to address unreliable submissions.
pts.d: Karlen bears responsibility for the brief filed in his name despite outsourcing its preparation, and loses appellate review while incurring a $10,000 damages obligation. Kruse and her counsel incur additional work identifying fictitious cases and responding to a meritless appeal; the damages partly compensate appellate fees and expenses. The court describes burdens on judicial resources and risks to judicial integrity. It acknowledges affordability barriers for self-represented litigants but does not find that AI resolves unmet legal need or relax procedural requirements for those unable to afford counsel. Its prospective warning expressly includes licensed lawyers as well as self-represented filers.
